exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables

question.text: Evaluate the gradient of $g(x,y)$ at the point $\left(e^2,1\right)$ if $g(x,y) =(x+y)(\ln x-y^2).$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives \begin{align} g_x(x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left((x+y)(\ln x-y^2)\right) \\[3pt] &=1\cdot(\ln x-y^2) + (x+y)\cdot \dfrac 1 x\\[3pt] &=\ln x-y^2 + 1+ \dfrac y x\\[7pt] g_y(x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left((x+y)(\ln x-y^2)\right) \\[3pt] &=1\cdot(\ln x-y^2)+ (x+y)\cdot(-2y) \\[3pt] &=\ln x-y^2-2xy-2y^2 \\[3pt] &=\ln x-3y^2-2xy \end{align}

Hence, the gradient is \begin{align} \nabla g(x,y) &=\left \langle g_x(x,y),\: g_y(x,y)\right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle \ln x-y^2 + 1+ \dfrac y x,\: \ln x-3y^2-2xy \right \rangle \\[7pt] \nabla g\left(e^2, 1\right)&=\left \langle \ln (e^2)-1^2 + 1+ \dfrac 1 {e^2},\: \ln (e^2)-3\cdot 1^2-2\cdot e^2\cdot 1 \right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle 2+ e^{-2},-1-2e^2 \right \rangle \end{align}

question.text: If $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x}e^{x/y},$ find $\nabla f(x,y).$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align} f_x (x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\dfrac {y}{x}e^{x/y}\right) \\[5pt] &=\left(-\dfrac {y}{x^2}+\dfrac{y}{x}\cdot\dfrac{1}{y}\right)e^{x/y} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac {x-y}{x^2}e^{x/y} \\[7pt] f_y (x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\dfrac {y}{x}e^{x/y}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac {1}{x}-\dfrac{y}{x}\cdot\dfrac{x}{y^2}\right)e^{x/y} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {y-x}{xy} e^{x/y} \end{align}

Hence, the gradient is \begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x (x,y)\ \mathbf i + f_y (x,y)\ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {x-y}{x^2}e^{x/y}\ \mathbf i +\dfrac {y-x}{xy} e^{x/y} \ \mathbf j . %&= \dfrac {x-y}{x^2}e^{x/y}\ \mathbf i -\dfrac {x-y}{xy} e^{x/y} \ \mathbf j \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables

question.text: Given $f(x,y) = \dfrac {3x+2y}{x-y}$, find $\nabla f(x,y).$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align} f_x (x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\dfrac {3x+2y}{x-y}\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac {3(x-y)-(3x+2y)}{(x-y)^2} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac {5y}{(x-y)^2} \\[7pt] f_y (x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\dfrac {3x+2y}{x-y}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {2(x-y)+(3x+2y)}{(x-y)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {5x}{(x-y)^2} \end{align}

Hence, the gradient is:

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x (x,y)\ \mathbf i + f_y (x,y)\ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac {5y}{(x-y)^2}\ \mathbf i +\dfrac {5x}{(x-y)^2} \ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac {5}{(x-y)^2}\ \left( y \ \mathbf i - x \ \mathbf j \right) \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y)$ at $(2,1)$ if $f(x,y) =x^2\sqrt{ y+3}.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align} f_x(x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(x^2\sqrt{ y+3}\right) \\[3pt] &=2x \sqrt {y+3} \\[7pt] f_y(x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(x^2\sqrt{ y+3}\right) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac {x^2}{2\sqrt{y+3}} . \end{align} Hence, the gradient is:

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &=\left \langle f_x(x,y), \:f_y(x,y) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle 2x \sqrt {y+3} ,\: \dfrac {x^2}{2\sqrt{y+3}} \right \rangle \\[7pt] \nabla f(2,1) &=\left \langle 2\cdot 2 \sqrt {1+3} , \: \dfrac {2^2}{2\sqrt{1+3}} \right \rangle \\[3pt] &= \left \langle 8, \:1 \right \rangle \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate $\nabla h(x,y)$ at $(1,1)$ if $h(x,y) =4x\arctan y.$
question.explanation: First, we find the partial derivatives \begin{align} h_x(x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(4x\arctan y\right) \\[3pt] &=4\arctan y \\[7pt] h_y(x,y)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(4x\arctan y\right) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac {4x}{y^2+1} \end{align} Hence, the gradient is \begin{align} \nabla h(x,y) &=\left \langle h_x(x,y), \:h_y(x,y) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle 4\arctan y, \: \dfrac {4x}{y^2+1} \right \rangle \\[7pt] \nabla h(1,1) &= \left \langle 4\arctan 1, \: \dfrac {4\cdot 1}{1^2+1} \right \rangle \\[3pt] &= \left \langle 4\cdot \dfrac \pi 4, \: \dfrac {4}{2} \right \rangle \\[3pt] &= \left \langle \pi , \: 2 \right \rangle . \end{align}

question.text: Given $g(x,y,z) = e^{2xz}\sin (y^2 - 1)$, find $\nabla g(x,y,z).$
question.choice1: $  2 e^{2xz}\  \left( z\sin (y^2 - 1)\mathbf i + y\cos(y^2-1)\ \mathbf j + x\sin (y^2 - 1)\ \mathbf k \right)$
question.choice2: $ z\sin (y^2 - 1)\mathbf i + y\cos(y^2-1)\ \mathbf j + x\sin (y^2 - 1)\ \mathbf k $
question.choice3: $ 2 e^{2xz}\  \left( z\mathbf i + y\ \mathbf j + x\ \mathbf k \right)$
question.choice4: $  2 e^{2xz}\sin (y^2 - 1)\  \left( z \mathbf i + y \ \mathbf j + x \ \mathbf k \right)$
question.choice5: $ 2 e^{2xz}\  \left( z\mathbf i + y\cos(y^2-1)\ \mathbf j + x\ \mathbf k \right)$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align} g_x (x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial x}\left( e^{2xz}\sin (y^2 - 1)\right) \\[3pt] &= 2z e^{2xz}\sin (y^2 - 1) \\[7pt] g_y (x,y,z)&=\dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(e^{2xz} \sin (y^2 - 1)\right) \\[3pt] &=2ye^{2xz}\cos(y^2-1)\\[7pt] g_z (x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(e^{2xz} \sin (y^2 - 1)\right) \\[3pt] &= 2x e^{2xz}\sin (y^2 - 1). \end{align}

Hence, the gradient is: \begin{align} \nabla g(x,y,z) &= g_x (x,y,z)\ \mathbf i +g_y (x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + g_z (x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[3pt] &= 2z e^{2xz}\sin (y^2 - 1)\ \mathbf i +2ye^{2xz}\cos(y^2-1)\ \mathbf j + 2x e^{2xz}\sin (y^2 - 1)\ \mathbf k \\[3pt] &= 2 e^{2xz}\ \left( z\sin (y^2 - 1)\mathbf i + y\cos(y^2-1)\ \mathbf j + x\sin (y^2 - 1)\ \mathbf k \right) \end{align}

question.text: Find $\nabla f(x,y,z) ,$ given that $ f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{1/2}}.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align} f_x (x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}\right) \\[5pt] %&=-\dfrac{1}{2(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\cdot 2x\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{x}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}} \\[7pt] f_y (x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}\right) \\[5pt] %&=-\dfrac{1}{2(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\cdot 2y\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{y}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}} \\[7pt] f_z (x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}\right) \\[5pt] %&=-\dfrac{1}{2(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\cdot 2z\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{z}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}. \end{align}

Hence, the gradient is \begin{align} \nabla f(x,y,z) &=f_x (x,y,z)\ \mathbf i + f_y (x,y,z)\ \mathbf j +f_z (x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &=\left(-\dfrac{x}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\right) \mathbf i +\left(-\dfrac{y}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\right) \mathbf j + \left(-\dfrac{z}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\right) \mathbf k\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\left(x \, \mathbf i +y \, \mathbf j + z \, \mathbf k\right) \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables

question.text: If $f(x,y,z) = x^y + y^z,$ find $\nabla f(x,y,z).$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} f_x (x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial x}(x^y+y^z) \\[5pt] %&= y\cdot x^{y-1}+0 \\[5pt] &= yx^{y-1} \\[7pt] f_y (x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial y}(x^y+y^z) \\[5pt] %&= \ln{x}\cdot x^y+z\cdot y^{z-1} \\[5pt] &= x^y\ln{x}+zy^{z-1} \\[7pt] f_z(x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial z}(x^y+y^z) \\[5pt] %&= 0+\ln{y}\cdot y^z \\[5pt] &= y^z\ln{y} \end{align*}

Hence, the gradient is \begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z) \, \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = yx^{y-1} \, \mathbf i + \left(x^y\ln{x}+zy^{z-1}\right) \mathbf j + y^z\ln{y} \, \mathbf k . \end{align*}

question.text: Find $\nabla g(x,y,z)$ given that $g(x,y,z) =\sqrt {x+2}+\ln(\sqrt{yz}).$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align} g_x(x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\sqrt {x+2}+\ln(\sqrt{yz})\right) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac 1 {2\sqrt{x+2}} + 0 \\[3pt] &= \dfrac 1 {2\sqrt{x+2}} \\[7pt] g_y(x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\sqrt {x+2}+\ln(\sqrt{yz})\right) \\[3pt] &= 0 + \dfrac 1 {\sqrt{yz}} \cdot \dfrac 1 {2\sqrt{yz}} \cdot z \\[3pt] &= \dfrac 1 {2y} \\[7pt] g_z(x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(\sqrt {x+2}+\ln(\sqrt{yz})\right) \\[3pt] &= 0 + \dfrac 1 {\sqrt{yz}} \cdot \dfrac 1 {2\sqrt{yz}} \cdot y \\[3pt] &= \dfrac 1 {2z} \end{align}

Hence, the gradient is: \begin{align} \nabla g(x,y,z) &=g_x(x,y,z)\ \mathbf i +g_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + g_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[3pt] &= \dfrac 1 {2\sqrt{x+2}}\mathbf i + \dfrac 1 {2y}\ \mathbf j + \dfrac 1 {2z}\ \mathbf k \end{align}

question.text: Find $\nabla g(x,y,z)$ given that $g(x,y,z) =x^2y^2z^2+e^{xyz}.$
question.choice5: $\left( xy^2z^2+yze^{xyz-1}\right)\ \mathbf  i + \left( x^2yz^2+xze^{xyz-1}\right)\ \mathbf j +\left(  x^2y^2z+xye^{xyz-1}\right)\ \mathbf k $
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align} g_x(x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(x^2y^2z^2+e^{xyz}\right) \\[3pt] &= 2xy^2z^2+yze^{xyz} \\[7pt] g_y(x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(x^2y^2z^2+e^{xyz}\right) \\[3pt] &= 2x^2yz^2+xze^{xyz} \\[7pt] g_z(x,y,z)&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(x^2y^2z^2+e^{xyz}\right) \\[3pt] &= 2x^2y^2z+xye^{xyz} \end{align}

Hence, the gradient is: \begin{align} \nabla g(x,y,z) &=g_x(x,y,z)\ \mathbf i +g_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + g_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[3pt] &= \left( 2xy^2z^2+yze^{xyz}\right)\ \mathbf i + \left( 2x^2yz^2+xze^{xyz}\right)\ \mathbf j + \left( 2x^2y^2z+xye^{xyz}\right)\ \mathbf k \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes

question.text: Given that $f(x,y) = x^2 - 2x\cos{y},$ find the points $(x, y),$ for $0\leq y\lt \pi,$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial x}(x^2-2x\cos{y}) \\[5pt] &=2x-2\cos{y}\\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial y}(x^2-2x\cos{y}) \\[5pt] %&= 0 +2x \sin{y} \\[5pt] &= 2x \sin{y} \end{align}

Hence, $\nabla f(x,y) =2(x-\cos{y}) \, \mathbf i +2x \sin{y} \, \mathbf j.$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

\[ 2(x-\cos{y}) \, \mathbf i + 2x \sin{y} \, \mathbf j = 0 \ \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j \]

So, by equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j},$ we obtain:

\[ \begin{cases} 2(x-\cos{y}) = 0 \\[5pt] 2x \sin{y} = 0 \end{cases} \]

From the first equation, we get $x=\cos{y}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain \begin{align*} %2x \sin{y} &=0\\[5pt] 2\cos{y}\sin{y} &= 0\\[5pt] \sin{2y} &=0\\[5pt] y & = 0, \, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{align*}

  • For $y=0,$ we get $x = \cos{0} = 1.$

  • For $y = \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ we get $x = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0.$

Therefore, $\nabla h(x,y) =\mathbf 0,$ for $0\leq y\lt \pi,$ at two points: $\left(1, 0 \right)$ and $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$

question.text: Given that $h(x,y)=(x^2-y^2)e^x$, find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla h(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial x}((x^2-y^2)e^x) \\[5pt] &= 2xe^x+(x^2-y^2)e^x\\[5pt] &= (x^2+2x-y^2)e^x \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial y}((x^2-y^2)e^x) \\[5pt] &= -2ye^x \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla h(x,y) = (x^2+2x-y^2)e^x \, \mathbf i -2ye^x \, \mathbf j.$

Now, we solve $\nabla h(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

\[ (x^2+2x-y^2)e^x \, \mathbf i -2ye^x \, \mathbf j = 0 \ \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j \]

So, by equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j},$ we obtain

\[ \begin{cases} (x^2+2x-y^2)e^x=0,\\[5pt] -2ye^x = 0. \end{cases} \] From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \begin{align*} (x^2+2x-0^2)e^x &=0\\[5pt] x(x + 2)e^{x} & = 0\\[5pt] x &=-2,\, 0. \end{align*}

Therefore, $\nabla h(x,y) =\mathbf 0$ at two points: $\left(-2, 0 \right)$ and $(0, 0).$

question.text: Given that $g(x,y)=4xy+y^2-x^2$, find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla g(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial x}(4xy+y^2-x^2) \\[3pt] &= 4y + 0 - 2x \\[3pt] &= 2(2y-x) \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial y}(4xy+y^2-x^2) \\[3pt] &= 4x+2y - 0 \\[3pt] &= 2(2x+y) \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla g(x,y) = 2(2y-x) \, \mathbf i + 2(2x+y) \, \mathbf j.$

Now, we solve $\nabla g(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

\[ 2(2y-x) \, \mathbf i + 2(2x+y) \, \mathbf j = 0 \ \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j \]

So, by equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j},$ we obtain:

\[ \begin{cases} 2y-x = 0 \\ 2x+y = 0 \end{cases} \] From the first equation, we get $x=2y.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: \begin{align*} 2(2y)+y &=0\\[3pt] 5y &= 0\\[3pt] y &=0 \end{align*}

Finally, we get $x = 2\cdot 0 = 0.$

Therefore, $\nabla g(x,y) =\mathbf 0$ at the point $(0, 0).$

question.text: Given that $g(x,y,z)= x\ln x + y\ln y + z\ln z -x -y -z$, find the points $(x, y, z)$ where $\nabla g(x,y,z) = \mathbf 0.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align} \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial x}\left( x\ln x + y\ln y + z\ln z -x -y -z \right) \\[3pt] &=\ln x + x\cdot \dfrac 1x + 0 + 0 -1 -0 -0 \\[3pt] &= \ln x + 1 - 1\\[3pt] &= \ln x\\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial y}\left( x\ln x + y\ln y + z\ln z -x -y -z \right) \\[3pt] &=0 + \ln y + y\cdot \dfrac 1y + 0 - 0 -1 -0 \\[3pt] &= \ln y + 1 - 1\\[3pt] &= \ln y\\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial z} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial z}\left( x\ln x + y\ln y + z\ln z -x -y -z \right) \\[3pt] &=0 + 0 + \ln z + z\cdot \dfrac 1z - 0 - 0 -1 \\[3pt] &= \ln z + 1 - 1\\[3pt] &= \ln z \end{align}

Hence, $\nabla g(x,y,z) =\ln x \, \mathbf{i} + \ln y \, \mathbf{j} + \ln z\, \mathbf{k}.$

Now, we solve $\nabla g(x,y,z) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \ln x \, \mathbf{i} + \ln y \, \mathbf{j} + \ln z \, \mathbf{k} &= 0 \ \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j + 0\ \mathbf j \end{align*}

So, by equating the coefficient of $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, and $\mathbf{k}$, we obtain: \[ \begin{cases} \ln x= 0 \\[5pt] \ln y = 0 \\[5pt] \ln z = 0 \end{cases} \]

From the first equation, we get $x = 1.$ Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain $y=1$ and $z=1.$

Hence, $\nabla g(x,y,z) = \mathbf 0$ at the point $(1,1,1).$

question.text: Given that $f(x,y,z)= \dfrac 1{xy} + \dfrac 1{y} + \dfrac 1{zx} - z$, find the points $(x, y, z)$ where $\nabla f(x,y,z) = \mathbf 0.$
question.explanation:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial x}\left( \dfrac 1{xy} + \dfrac 1{y} + \dfrac 1{zx} - z \right) \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac1{x^2y} + 0 - \dfrac1{zx^2} - 0 \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{z+y}{x^2yz}\\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial y}\left( \dfrac 1{xy} + \dfrac 1{y} + \dfrac 1{zx} - z \right) \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac1{xy^2} - \dfrac1{y^2} + 0 - 0 \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1+x}{xy^2}\\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} &= \dfrac {\partial }{\partial z}\left( \dfrac 1{xy} + \dfrac 1{y} + \dfrac 1{zx} - z \right) \\[5pt] &=0 + 0 - \dfrac1{z^2x} - 1 \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1 + z^2x}{z^2x} \end{align}

Hence, $\nabla f(x,y,z) = -\dfrac{z+y}{x^2yz} \, \mathbf{i} -\dfrac{1+x}{xy^2} \, \mathbf{j} -\dfrac{1 + z^2x}{z^2x}\, \mathbf{k}.$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y,z) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} -\dfrac{z+y}{x^2yz} \, \mathbf{i} -\dfrac{1+x}{xy^2} \, \mathbf{j} -\dfrac{1 + z^2x}{z^2x} \, \mathbf{k} &= 0 \ \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j + 0\ \mathbf j \end{align*}

So, by equating the coefficient of $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, and $\mathbf{k}$, we obtain: \[ \begin{cases} -\dfrac{z+y}{x^2yz}= 0 \\[5pt] -\dfrac{1+x}{xy^2} = 0 \\[5pt] -\dfrac{1 + z^2x}{z^2x} = 0 \end{cases} \]

From the second equation, we get $x = -1.$ Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain: \begin{align*} -\dfrac{1 + z^2x}{z^2x} &= 0\\[5pt] -\dfrac{1 + z^2(-1)}{z^2(-1)} & = 0\\[5pt] 1 - z^2 &= 0\\[3pt] z^2 & = 1\\[3pt] z &= \pm 1 \end{align*}

Substituting $x = -1$ into the first equation, we obtain: \begin{align*} -\dfrac{z+y}{(-1)^2yz}&= 0 \\[5pt] z + y &= 0\\[3pt] y &= - z \end{align*}

When $z = 1,$ we have $y = -1$ and when $z=-1,$ we have $y = 1.$

Hence, $\nabla f(x,y,z) = \mathbf 0$ at two points: $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(-1,1,-1).$

question.text: Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that \begin{align*} f(x,y) & = \arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right), \qquad && \nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x^2+y^2}\, \mathbf i - \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \, \mathbf j, && \\[5pt] h(x,y) & = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \qquad && \nabla h(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf j. && \end{align*}
question.explanation:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by \[ \nabla [fh] = h \nabla f + f \nabla h. \]

Using the product rule, we obtain \begin{align*} \nabla [f(x,y) h(x,y) ] & = h (x,y) \nabla f(x,y) + f(x,y) \nabla h(x,y)\\[5pt] & = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\left( \dfrac{y}{x^2+y^2}\, \mathbf i - \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \, \mathbf j \right) + \arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)\left( \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf j \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{y\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{x^2+y^2}\, \mathbf i - \dfrac{x\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{x^2+y^2} \, \mathbf j + \dfrac{x\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{y\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\, \mathbf i - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \, \mathbf j + \dfrac{x\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{y\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{y + x\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\, \mathbf i + \dfrac{y\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) - x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} \left( \left( y + x\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( y\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) - x \right)\mathbf{j} \right). \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient

question.text: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y) g(x,y)$ if $f(x,y) = e^{x+y}$ and $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2?$
question.explanation:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

\[ \nabla [fg] = f \, \nabla\! g+ g \, \nabla\! f \]

First, we calculate the first order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(e^{x+y}\right) =e^{x+y} \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(e^{x+y}\right) =e^{x+y} \end{align*}

Hence, \begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}\ \mathbf j =e^{x+y} \ \mathbf i + e^{x+y} \ \mathbf j . \end{align*}

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial x}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^2+y^2\right) = 2x \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial y}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( x^2+y^2\right) = 2y \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \nabla g(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial x}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial g}{\partial y}\ \mathbf j =2x\ \mathbf i +2y \ \mathbf j . \end{align*}

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \nabla [f(x,y) g(x,y)] &= (e^{x+y})(2x\ \mathbf i +2y \ \mathbf j ) + \left(x^2+y^2\right)\left(e^{x+y}\ \mathbf i + e^{x+y} \ \mathbf j \right) \\[3pt] &=2xe^{x+y}\ \mathbf i +2ye^{x+y} \ \mathbf j + \left(x^2+y^2\right)e^{x+y} \ \mathbf i +\left(x^2+y^2\right)e^{x+y}\ \mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \left(x^2+2x+y^2\right)e^{x+y} \ \mathbf i + \left(x^2+2y+y^2\right)e^{x+y}\ \mathbf j \end{align*}

question.text: Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that \begin{align*} f(x,y) &= x^2y+xy^2, \qquad && \nabla f(x,y) = (2xy+y^2)\ \mathbf i + (x^2+2xy) \ \mathbf j, && \\[3pt] h(x,y) &= \dfrac1{xy}, \qquad && \nabla h(x,y) = -\dfrac1{x^2y} \ \mathbf i - \dfrac1{xy^2}\ \mathbf j. && \end{align*}
question.explanation:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

\[ \nabla [fh] = h \, \nabla\! f + f \, \nabla\! h \]

Using the product rule, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \nabla [f(x,y) h(x,y) ] & = h (x,y) \nabla f(x,y) + f(x,y) \nabla h(x,y)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1{xy}((2xy+y^2)\ \mathbf i + (x^2+2xy) \ \mathbf j ) + (x^2y+xy^2)\left(-\dfrac1{x^2y} \ \mathbf i - \dfrac1{xy^2}\ \mathbf j \right) \\[5pt] & = \left(\dfrac{2xy+y^2}{xy}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac{x^2+2xy}{xy} \ \mathbf j \right) + \left(-\dfrac{x^2y+xy^2}{x^2y} \ \mathbf i - \dfrac{x^2y+xy^2}{xy^2}\ \mathbf j \right) \\[5pt] & =\left(\dfrac{2x+y}{x}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac{x+2y}{y}\ \mathbf j \right) + \left(-\dfrac{x+y}{x}\ \mathbf i - \dfrac{x+y}{y}\ \mathbf j \right) \\[5pt] &= \left( -\dfrac{x+y}{x} + \dfrac{2x+y}{x} \right) \ \mathbf i + \left( -\dfrac{x+y}{y} + \dfrac{x+2y}{y} \right)\ \mathbf j\\[5pt] &= \ \mathbf i + \ \mathbf j \end{align*}

question.text: Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that \begin{align*} f(x,y) &= {x+y}, \quad && \nabla f(x,y) = \ \mathbf i + \ \mathbf j, && \\[3pt] g(x,y) &= \ln(x+y), \quad && \nabla g(x,y) = \dfrac1{x+y}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac 1{x+y}\ \mathbf j. && \end{align*}
question.explanation:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

\[ \nabla [fg] = g \, \nabla\! f + f \, \nabla\! g \]

So, using this product rule we obtain:

\begin{align*} \nabla [f(x,y) g(x,y) ] & = g (x,y) \nabla f(x,y) + f(x,y) \nabla g(x,y)\\[5pt] &=\ln(x+y)(\ \mathbf i + \ \mathbf j) + (x+y)\left( \dfrac1{x+y}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac 1{x+y} \ \mathbf j\right) \\[5pt] & =\ln(x+y) \ \mathbf i + \ln(x+y)\ \mathbf j + \dfrac{x+y}{x+y}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac{x+y}{x+y} \ \mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \left( \ln(x+y)\ \mathbf i + \ \mathbf i \right) + \left( \ln(x+y)\ \mathbf j + 1 \ \mathbf j \right) \\[5pt] & =(\ln(x+y)+1) \ \mathbf i + (\ln(x+y)+1)\ \mathbf j \end{align*}

question.text: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z) h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z) = xyz$ and $h(x,y,z) = \ln(xyz)?$
question.explanation:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by \[ \nabla [fh] = f \nabla h+ h \nabla f . \]

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( xyz \right) =yz \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(xyz\right) =xz \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(xyz\right) =xy \end{align*}

Hence, \begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}\ \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z}\ \mathbf k = yz \ \mathbf i +xz \ \mathbf j +xy \ \mathbf k . \end{align*}

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial x}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( \ln{(xyz)}\right) =\dfrac{1}{x} \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial y}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y}\left( \ln{(xyz)}\right) =\dfrac{1}{y}\\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial z}&= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z}\left( \ln{(xyz)}\right) =\dfrac{1}{z} \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \nabla h(x,y,z) &= \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial x}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial y}\ \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial h}{\partial z}\ \mathbf k\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{x}\ \mathbf i +\dfrac{1}{y} \ \mathbf j +\dfrac{1}{z} \ \mathbf k. \end{align*}

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain \begin{align*} \nabla [f(x,y,z) h(x,y,z) ] & = f(x,y,z) \nabla h(x,y,z) + h (x,y,z) \nabla f(x,y,z) \\[5pt] & = xyz\left( \dfrac{1}{x}\ \mathbf i +\dfrac{1}{y} \ \mathbf j +\dfrac{1}{z} \ \mathbf k \right) + \ln(xyz)\left( yz \ \mathbf i +xz \ \mathbf j +xy \ \mathbf k \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{xyz}{x}\ \mathbf i + \dfrac{xyz}{y} \ \mathbf j +\dfrac{xyz}{z} \ \mathbf k + \ln(xyz)\left( yz \ \mathbf i +xz \ \mathbf j +xy \ \mathbf k \right)\\[5pt] & = yz \ \mathbf i + xz \ \mathbf j + xy \ \mathbf k + \ln(xyz)\left( yz \ \mathbf i +xz \ \mathbf j +xy \ \mathbf k \right)\\[5pt] & = (1 + \ln(xyz)) \left( yz \ \mathbf i +xz \ \mathbf j +xy \ \mathbf k \right). \end{align*}
